problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=1\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\textrm m,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$
